objective: By the end of this lesson you can teach the oxygen rules from the words of 14 CFR 91.211 and 61.31(g), teach a learner to recognize hypoxia and budget the time of useful consciousness, brief and operate oxygen equipment as a demonstration, and work out the oxygen a scenario needs.
why: Hypoxia attacks judgment first, and AC 61-107B calls the belief that it is easy to recognize and correct a dangerous misconception [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Your learners will believe that belief until you teach them otherwise, and for pressurized airplanes above 25,000 ft your signature is what lets them act as pilot in command [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]].

prereading.what: The oxygen rule itself. Read it as your learners never do: cabin pressure altitude, required minimum flight crew, provided with and uses.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.211

prereading.what: The high-altitude training and endorsement you may give: nine ground subjects, three flight subjects, and who is excepted.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 61.31(g)

prereading.what: Physiological training: gas laws, hypoxia types, signs versus symptoms, prevention, treatment, decompression and the TUC table. The core of this lesson.
prereading.label: AC 61-107B 2-7

prereading.what: DCS rules of thumb, FAA physiological training at CAMI, and oxygen equipment, fire risk and inspection.
prereading.label: AC 61-107B 2-8 to 2-9

prereading.what: Decompression, oxygen systems, masks, cannulas, pulse oximeters and servicing.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-36 to 7-40

prereading.what: Effects of altitude, the FAA oxygen recommendation, chamber training, and the hyperventilation rule for a pilot already on oxygen.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-2 to 8-1-3

prereading.what: Demonstration-performance and telling-and-doing: the method you will use to teach the oxygen equipment.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-8

warmup: Think first: a learner tells you he never needs oxygen below 14,000 ft because on a mountain hike he could feel the altitude, so he would know if he were hypoxic. Which words in AC 61-107B would you show him, what could he learn in an altitude chamber that he cannot learn on a hike, and how would you teach him to use the oxygen system without waiting to feel anything?

key_terms.def: The crew 91.211(a)(1) and (a)(2) make provide for and use oxygen. Passengers are not part of it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].
Oxygen is available to the person. Above 15,000 ft cabin pressure altitude 91.211(a)(3) requires this for each occupant, not use [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].
Something an observer can detect, such as rapid breathing, cyanosis or poor coordination. Signs do not help the hypoxic person recognize it in themselves [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
A sensation the hypoxic person can detect, such as air hunger, headache, tingling or euphoria [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
The order and intensity of a person's own symptoms, which usually stay the same over the years. Learning it is the main benefit of chamber training [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Also called effective performance time. The time from losing the oxygen supply to when a person can no longer take proper corrective and protective action [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
A gradual loss of cabin pressure. AC 61-107B calls slow decompressions the most dangerous, because hypoxia dulls the mind before anyone notices [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
A hypobaric chamber flight that lets a pilot experience hypoxia. Highly recommended but required by no regulation [[11:17|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

The logbook or training record endorsement 14 CFR 61.31(g) requires before a person acts as PIC of a pressurized aircraft with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]].
Oxygen that meets or exceeds SAE AS8010, the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard. AC 61-107B says only this oxygen should be used [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].
Oxygen equipment carried for passengers' medical use. Part 135 sets conditions on its type, marking, condition and stowage [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]].
A medical device that separates oxygen from other gases in ambient air and dispenses the concentrated oxygen to the user [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks of an instructor

body.p: As a commercial pilot you learned to plan and fly with oxygen. As an instructor you teach it to people who cannot yet feel what hypoxia does to them, and you may sign the endorsement that lets a pilot fly a pressurized airplane high. The rule behind that endorsement grew out of NTSB safety recommendations made in 1982 after a series of fatal accidents that the NTSB believed involved a lack of high-altitude knowledge and proficiency [[11:9|AC 61-107B 1-7]].

14 CFR 61.31(g)(1) bars a person from acting as PIC of a pressurized aircraft (one whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL) until that person has received and logged ground training from an authorized instructor and has an endorsement for it. The ground training must include at least these subjects [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]:

bullets: High-altitude aerodynamics and meteorology
Respiration
Effects, symptoms and causes of hypoxia and any other high-altitude sickness
Duration of consciousness without supplemental oxygen
Effects of prolonged usage of supplemental oxygen
Causes and effects of gas expansion and gas bubble formation
Preventive measures for gas expansion, gas bubble formation and high-altitude sickness
Physical phenomena and incidents of decompression
Any other physiological aspects of high-altitude flight

body.p: 61.31(g)(2) adds flight training in a pressurized aircraft or a representative simulator or training device, with an endorsement of proficiency. It must include normal cruise above 25,000 ft MSL, proper emergency procedures for a simulated rapid decompression without actually depressurizing the aircraft, and emergency descent procedures [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]. A pilot who can document certain earlier experience in a pressurized aircraft, such as PIC before April 15, 1991, a military PIC check, or a part 121, 125 or 135 PIC proficiency check, is excepted [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31]].

AC 61-107B Chapter 2 is an outline of training that meets 61.31(g), and the instructor who gives it endorses the pilot's logbook or training record [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. AC 61-65K gives the sample wording: the pilot received the required training of 61.31(g) in a named make and model of pressurized aircraft, and you found the pilot proficient in its operation and systems [[12:54|AC 61-65K A.74]].

callout.text: 61.31(g) applies only to those pressurized airplanes, but AC 61-107B highly recommends the same training for every pilot who flies above 10,000 ft MSL [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]]. Offer the ground portion to any learner who will use oxygen.

check.q: A pressurized single has a service ceiling of 27,000 ft and a maximum operating altitude of 25,000 ft. Does 61.31(g) apply to its pilots?
check.a: No. The rule looks at the lower of the two numbers, and that number must be above 25,000 ft MSL. Here the lower is 25,000 ft, which is not above it [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]. AC 61-107B still recommends the training [[11:10|AC 61-107B 2-1]].

chunks.title: K1: Teach 91.211 from the rule's own words

body.p: Most learners meet the oxygen rule in a handbook summary. The PHAK says flight crews must have and use oxygen after 30 minutes 'between 12,500 and 14,000 feet' and that every occupant above 15,000 ft 'must have' it [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. That is close, but it is not the rule. Teach from 14 CFR 91.211, phrase by phrase [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

head: Phrase in 91.211
What learners often think
What the rule says
rows: Cabin pressure altitudes
The altitude the airplane is flying at
The trigger is the pressure altitude inside the cabin, in feet MSL [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Above 12,500 feet up to and including 14,000 feet
'Between' the two numbers
Exactly 12,500 ft is outside the band; exactly 14,000 ft is inside it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Required minimum flight crew
Every pilot on board
Only the crew the aircraft requires; a passenger who is a pilot is still a passenger [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Is provided with and uses
Has oxygen on board
Must have it and breathe it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
That part of the flight at those altitudes that is of more than 30 minutes duration
Oxygen after 30 minutes of total flight
Only the time in the band beyond the first 30 minutes there [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Each occupant of the aircraft is provided with
Passengers must wear oxygen above 15,000 ft
Passengers must have it available; the rule does not make them use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]

body.p: Paragraph (b) adds the pressurized rules: above FL 250 a 10-minute supply for each occupant, on top of paragraph (a), for a descent after losing pressurization [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]], and above FL 350 one pilot at the controls wearing a sealed mask, with a quick-donning exception up to FL 410 for two pilots [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211]].

callout.text: Teach this as a short talk followed by discussion: give the basic rule, then have the learner read each phrase aloud and argue what it means [[25:116|AIH 5-13]]. Learners who understand the purpose behind each step remember it better and can rebuild it when they forget [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

check.q: A learner says passengers above 15,000 ft must wear oxygen. Which words in 91.211 do you point to?
check.a: Paragraph (a)(3) says each occupant must be 'provided with' supplemental oxygen. Only (a)(1) and (a)(2) say the required minimum flight crew must be provided with and 'use' it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

chunks.title: K2a: Impairment starts before the learner notices

body.p: Impairment is the part of hypoxia to teach first. About 20 percent of the oxygen you inhale feeds the brain, so the brain is among the first organs affected, and its higher reasoning parts degrade first: judgment and cognitive skills diminish from the very start [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

bullets: From 12,000 to 15,000 ft, judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and the ability to calculate are impaired, and performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes at 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].

There is no definite altitude where impairment begins. AC 61-107B calls it a continuum, gives no assurance that 12,000 ft is always safe, and recommends descending below 10,000 ft MSL when hypoxia is suspected [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

Impairment increases with altitude, with harder and more complex tasks, and with new tasks compared to learned, practiced ones [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. A learner on a first high flight is doing new tasks.

Carbon monoxide, anemia, some medicines, small amounts of alcohol, heat, cold, fever and anxiety lower the altitude where hypoxia bites [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. A smoker's physiological altitude at sea level is about 7,000 ft, and 20,000 ft for a nonsmoker is like 22,000 ft for a smoker [[11:24|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

Fatigue can be intensified by hypoxia [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. The AIH warns that late nights, fatigue and sustained flight above 5,000 ft can make a pilot less critical, less decisive and more accepting just as the approach arrives [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

callout.text: AC 61-107B: it is a common misconception that hypoxia is easy to recognize and correct before serious impairment, and that idea is misleading and dangerous [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Make this the headline of your lesson.

Because the learner's judgment is what fails, give rules that do not depend on judgment: the FAA recommends supplemental oxygen on any unpressurized flight to or above 10,000 ft by day or above 5,000 ft at night [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Have the learner put oxygen on at a planned altitude, not when it feels needed (application).

check.q: Why is a learner on a first high-altitude flight more at risk of impairment than a pilot who flies high every week?
check.a: AC 61-107B says impairment increases with new tasks compared to learned, practiced ones, and with harder, more complex tasks [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: K2b: Symptoms of hypoxia: signs you see, symptoms they feel

body.p: Symptoms of hypoxia are the sensations a hypoxic person can detect. Signs are what an observer can see, and they are not much use to the hypoxic person [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. That split is made for instructors: you are the observer in the right seat.

bullets: Most hypoxic people get the same symptoms, but in a different order and intensity. A person's own order and intensity usually stay the same over the years, so knowing your 'signature' helps you recognize hypoxia in flight [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The AIM says the same: symptoms do not vary in an individual [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

Euphoria, a false sense of well-being, is probably the most dangerous symptom. Visual impairment is probably the least reliable, because the visual field changes so slowly it can go unnoticed [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

Apart from possible headache and nausea there are no other uncomfortable symptoms, and onset is usually insidious; being busy with flying duties can let hypoxia go beyond self-help [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

The PHAK adds decreased response to stimuli, longer reaction time, drowsiness, numbness and a narrowing field of vision, and warns that hypoxia can make a pilot believe everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

Hyperventilation looks the same and is an early response to hypoxia at altitude. AC 61-107B treats both at once: 100 percent oxygen under pressure, slower and shallower breathing, check the equipment, descend [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
After an extreme exposure, 100 percent oxygen can seem to make symptoms worse for 15 to 60 seconds. Keep breathing 100 percent, slowly [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

callout.text: Above 10,000 ft, watch your learner for the signs column: rapid breathing, bluish skin, poor coordination, lethargy, poor judgment, sweating, trembling, muscle spasms [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Ask the learner to watch you too, and to say what they feel (application).

check.q: Which can you, the instructor, detect in a learner: poor coordination or air hunger?
check.a: Poor coordination is a sign, which an observer can detect. Air hunger is a symptom, which only the learner can feel [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: K2c: Time of useful consciousness, taught as a budget

body.p: Time of useful consciousness (TUC), also called effective performance time, runs from the loss of the oxygen supply to the moment a person can no longer take proper corrective and protective action [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. The PHAK calls it the most time a pilot has to make rational, life-saving decisions and carry them out [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. It is not the time until unconsciousness: impaired performance may be immediate [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

bullets: The values are averages with wide variation between people, so AC 61-107B says to assume the lower value is the one that limits you [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

A rapid decompression between 25,000 and 43,000 ft cuts TUC by about 50 percent. Above 43,000 ft TUC falls to about 9 to 12 seconds, the time for blood to travel from lung to brain plus the brain's reserve [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

TUC also drops with a faster ascent, physical activity (10 deep knee bends at 25,000 ft without a mask cut it by 50 percent), fatigue, low blood sugar, alcohol, some medicines, smoking, poor condition and illness [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Because the potential for impairment begins almost at once, the AC says to practice donning the oxygen mask from time to time [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

callout.text: Teach TUC as a budget. Table 2-6 gives 5 seconds or less to don the mask [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]; at 25,000 ft after a rapid decompression the lower value is 1.5 minutes [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Ask the learner how much of that budget a search for the mask would use (application).

check.q: At 28,000 ft, what TUC should a learner plan on, and why that number?
check.a: 2.5 minutes, the lower end of 2.5 to 3 minutes, because AC 61-107B says to assume the lower value is limiting [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: Physiological training: the chamber and the ground lesson

body.p: Part 91 and part 125 have no specific physiological training requirement. 61.31(g) requires the high-altitude training in AC 61-107B, and parts 121 and 135 require physiology training for crew above 25,000 ft MSL, but none of the regulations include altitude chamber training [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]]. AC 61-107B still calls chamber training highly recommended for all pilots [[11:17|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

bullets: The FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute (CAMI) gives a one-day aviation physiology course with a rapid decompression from 8,000 to 18,000 ft MSL and a hypoxia demonstration at 25,000 ft MSL in a hypobaric chamber, plus a spatial disorientation demonstrator [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]] [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]].
Trainees must be at least 18, hold a current medical certificate (at least third class for the chamber) and be free of a cold or other significant health problem [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]].
Allow at least 24 hours between hypobaric chamber exposure and flying [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
The AIM says experiencing hypoxia in a chamber flight greatly improves recognition, and names CAMI and many military facilities [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

AC 61-107B lists an FAA physiology of flight video library for ground training [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]], and says ground training should include the history and causes of past accidents [[11:12|AC 61-107B 2-3]].

head: Gas law
What it explains for the learner
rows: Dalton's law
Hypoxia: lower total pressure means a lower partial pressure of oxygen [[11:18|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Boyle's law
Trapped gas expanding in ears, sinuses and the GI tract [[11:18|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Henry's law
Decompression sickness: nitrogen leaves solution and can form bubbles [[11:18|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Graham's law
Gas transfer between air, lungs, blood and cells [[11:17|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Charles' law
No physiological bearing, since body temperature stays constant [[11:18|AC 61-107B 2-7]]

callout.text: The law of intensity says a dramatic, real experience teaches more than a routine one [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. A chamber flight is that experience. On the ground, an accident report read as a scenario is the next best thing [[11:12|AC 61-107B 2-3]].

check.q: A learner books a chamber flight for 0800 and a cross-country for 1300 the same day. What do you tell him?
check.a: Move one of them. AC 61-107B says to allow at least 24 hours between hypobaric chamber exposure and flying [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: K3a: Continuous flow, demand and pressure-demand systems

body.p: Learners group things that share attributes into concepts [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. Give them one question that sorts every system: when does oxygen flow? All the time, only when you inhale, or when you inhale and under pressure. The ACS says 'demand'; the PHAK and AC 61-107B call it diluter demand [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

head: System
Characteristics
Limitations
Applicability
rows: Continuous flow
Flows at a rate set automatically or by the user; the user exhales around the facepiece; a rebreather bag [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Certificated to 41,000 ft MSL, but needs very careful attention above 25,000 ft MSL [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Usually for passengers [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]; pilot masks sometimes allow more flow, so pilots use theirs [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Diluter demand (demand)
Flows only when the user inhales; an automix lever mixes cabin air and oxygen, or gives 100 percent [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Tight seal needed; safe up to 40,000 ft MSL; air seeps in past beards and mustaches [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Crew masks fitted with little leakage, usually with a microphone [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Pressure demand
Like diluter demand, plus positive pressure to the facepiece that pressurizes the lungs with oxygen, above 34,000 ft cabin altitude [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Safe above 40,000 ft MSL [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Very high altitudes; a mask-mounted regulator avoids a long hose that must be purged [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]

body.p: The PHAK adds a fourth, portable type the ACS does not name: electrical pulse demand, which gives oxygen only at the start of each breath and can use 50 to 85 percent less than continuous flow [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]. Whatever the type, the most important thing is that the mask and the system are compatible [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

callout.text: Teach on the real regulator. At high altitude, crewmembers should select the 100 percent setting on a demand or pressure-demand regulator [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. The AFM or oxygen supplement gives the switch positions for your airplane.

check.q: What one question sorts a system into continuous flow or demand?
check.a: Does oxygen flow all the time, or only when the user inhales through the mask? [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]

chunks.title: K3b: Aviator's breathing oxygen and other types of oxygen

body.p: The differences between aviator's breathing oxygen and other types start with one standard. Aircraft containers should be supplied with oxygen that meets or exceeds SAE AS8010 (as revised), the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]], and AC 61-107B says only that oxygen should be used [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

head: Type of oxygen
What the sources say
Identification
rows: Aviator's breathing oxygen
Meets or exceeds SAE AS8010 [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Ask for a fill that meets SAE AS8010 and check the supplier's paperwork (application; the sources give no marking)
Medical oxygen carried for a passenger (Part 135)
Equipment of an approved type or meeting the 49 CFR marking and labeling rules, free of flammable contaminants outside, valves and gauges protected, secured [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]]
By its approval or its 49 CFR markings and labels [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]]
Portable oxygen concentrator
A medical device that separates oxygen from other gases in ambient air [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]
It makes oxygen from cabin air instead of carrying a high-pressure supply [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]
Shop or welding oxygen
Not named in these sources
Not shown to meet SAE AS8010, so it fails the AC's 'only' test (application)

callout.text: Teach the right source the first time. By the law of primacy, what is learned first makes a strong, almost unshakable impression [[25:64|AIH 3-13]], so the first bottle a learner sees filled should come with the SAE AS8010 question.

check.q: What is the one test AC 61-107B gives for oxygen that goes into an aircraft system?
check.a: It meets or exceeds SAE AS8010, the Aviator's Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

chunks.title: K3c and R3: Precautions and compressed gas containers

body.p: Precautions when using supplemental oxygen systems start with the container. Aircraft oxygen is usually stored at 1,800 to 2,200 psi [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. Teach the learner to treat the bottle as stored energy.

head: Precaution
Source
rows: Fasten the container securely before flight
Secure loose items, oxygen cylinders included, so an explosive decompression cannot turn them into flying debris
Mark a high-pressure container with its psi tolerance before filling it to that pressure
Never let cylinder pressure exceed the rated cylinder pressure (the Part 135 medical oxygen rule)
A lower gauge reading on a cold day may be temperature, not a leak
The aircraft system inspected by a certified maintenance provider and the bottles hydrostatically tested by a DOT-approved facility before use
Portable equipment readily accessible in flight
Preflight with clean hands: mask and tubing, regulator, quantity, gauges, flow indicators and connections; don and test; all valves off after use

callout.text: A loose bottle is a hazard twice: a missile in an explosive decompression [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]], and out of reach when the learner needs it in seconds [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
Teach the preflight with learner tells, instructor does: the learner talks you through each item while you do it, so you can correct a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: A learner wants the oxygen bottle loose on the rear seat so passengers can reach it. Your answer?
check.a: Fasten it securely before flight [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. In an explosive decompression an unsecured cylinder becomes flying debris [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]]. Find a secured spot that is still readily accessible.

chunks.title: R4: Combustion hazards in an oxygen-rich environment

body.p: Oxygen raises the fire risk of everything around it. Materials nearly fireproof in ordinary air may burn in oxygen, oils and greases may catch fire if exposed to it and cannot be used to seal oxygen valves and fittings, and smoking while any oxygen equipment is in use must be strictly forbidden [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]] [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

bullets: Oxygen under pressure reacts spontaneously with petroleum products. Wash dirt, oil and grease, including lip salve and hair oil, off your hands, and keep clothing and tools clean [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
Service oxygen only outside the hangar [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]], not during fueling or other work that could make a spark, and not with passengers aboard [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]].
If a fire breaks out at high altitude, descend at once to an altitude that does not require oxygen and follow the AFM [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-11d]].
Part 135 sets a distance for medical oxygen: no smoking or open flame within 10 feet of it [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]].

callout.text: Oxygen is the fire's helper: anything oily or burning near it burns harder [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].
Put the hidden fuels into your passenger briefing by name: lip balm, hair oil and greasy hands [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]. Learners rarely think of cosmetics as petroleum products (application).

check.q: Why does AC 61-107B say to descend to an altitude that does not require oxygen if a fire starts at high altitude?
check.a: Because of the highly combustible composition of oxygen; once lower, the oxygen no longer needs to flow [[11:43|AC 61-107B 2-11d]].

chunks.title: R1 and R2: High altitude flight and use of supplemental oxygen

body.p: High altitude flight: the risk your learner underrates is the quiet one. During a slow decompression the noise, fog and wind blast may not happen, and hypoxia dulls the mind that should notice, so AC 61-107B calls slow decompressions the most dangerous [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Automatic warnings generally give the first indication [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

bullets: A small pressurized cabin can decompress 10 to 200 times faster than a large one [[11:41|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].
If pressurization depends on the turbocharger compressor, a turbocharger failure can cost cabin pressure; watch the cabin during the descent [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

Use of supplemental oxygen: do not let a pulse oximeter be the only hypoxia indicator. Waiting for its number to fall can let impairment set in, and a fingertip reading may not show the brain's real oxygen [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

Altitude DCS is a risk every time you fly unpressurized above 18,000 ft. Avoid strenuous activity before such a flight and for 24 hours after; breathing 100 percent oxygen in flight without prebreathing does not prevent DCS [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
After an in-flight rapid decompression, do not fly for at least 24 hours [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

With no supplemental oxygen, start an emergency descent to below 10,000 ft MSL [[11:23|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. A rapid descent can cold-shock a piston engine, but a safe altitude comes first [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

body.p: When you teach the emergency descent, follow the manufacturer. Simulated descents should be made in a turn to check for traffic below and look for a landing area, with a 30 to 45 degree bank to keep positive load factors [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

check.q: Why does AC 61-107B call a slow decompression the most dangerous kind?
check.a: Its phenomena may not be evident, and hypoxia depresses the mental function needed to recognize the emergency and start recovery [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: S1 briefing and S2 operating the equipment

body.p: Oxygen equipment is a procedure, so teach it with telling-and-doing, on the ground first, with the real equipment [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Demonstrate it exactly the way you want the learner to do it, because learners imitate the instructor [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

head: Step
With the oxygen equipment
rows: Instructor tells, instructor does
Preflight, don, check flow and shut off while explaining each step [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner talks you through it; you see what they understand and fix errors before they touch it [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner tells, learner does
The learner does it, thinking aloud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner does, instructor evaluates
The learner briefs and operates it with no prompting [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]

body.p: S1, the briefing. Cover these, in this order:

bullets: When oxygen goes on: at a planned altitude, per the FAA recommendation of above 10,000 ft by day and 5,000 ft at night [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
How: don the mask or cannula and check flow, such as the green flow detector or the reservoir bag [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
If symptoms appear while on oxygen: regulator to 100 percent, then check the system, then slow the breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].
No smoking, and no oil, grease or lip balm near the equipment [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]] [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].
The emergency drill: mask on in 5 seconds or less, check flow, breathe 100 percent; descend; land as soon as possible where medical help is available [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

body.p: S2, operating the equipment. The AFH training outline lists a functional test of supply and pressure, regulator operation, oxygen flow, mask fit, and talking to the other pilot and ATC through the mask microphones [[24:309|AFH 15-15]]. Preflight it so it is ready the moment the mask goes on [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]], and shut every valve after use [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. With no installed or portable equipment, simulate each step aloud.

callout.text: In 61.31(g) flight training the rapid decompression is simulated without actually depressurizing the aircraft [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]. The AFH outline pairs it with the immediate donning of oxygen masks [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].
A learner donning a mask in flight is not flying. Brief who has the controls and use the positive exchange of flight controls before every donning drill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Why have the learner tell you the oxygen preflight while you do it?
check.a: Freed from doing it, the learner can organize the steps, and you can judge their understanding and correct it before they become absorbed in doing it [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: S3: Working the evaluator's oxygen quantity scenario

body.p: Teach one method and use it every time. AC 61-107B has the trainee calculate oxygen requirements from the AFM during preflight planning [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

bullets: 1. Write the profile by cabin pressure altitude and minutes in each band [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].
2. Crew: above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 ft, only the minutes beyond 30; above 14,000 ft, every minute [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].
3. Occupants: provided with oxygen for every minute above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].
4. Pressurized above FL 250: add a 10-minute supply for each occupant [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].
5. Add what the FAA recommends (above 10,000 ft by day, 5,000 ft at night) and a margin [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].
6. Turn person-minutes into supply with the AFM or system maker's chart, and compare it to the gauge, allowing for a cold soak [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

body.p: Worked example (application). Unpressurized, by day, one pilot and two passengers: 90 minutes at 13,500 ft, then 40 minutes at 15,500 ft.

head: Who
91.211 minimum
With the FAA recommendation
rows: Pilot
130 min
Each passenger
40 min provided, above 15,000 ft only [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
130 min
Total person-minutes

body.p: AC 61-107B gives one sizing example: a typical 22 cubic ft portable container holds about 1.5 hours at 18,000 ft MSL for four people [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. That is 22 / (4 x 1.5) = about 3.67 cubic ft per person-hour, for that example only.

callout.text: Plan to the recommendation, not to the rule's minimum: the FAA recommendation in the example more than doubles the supply.

check.q: In the worked example, why do the passengers need only 40 minutes by rule while the pilot needs 100?
check.a: Occupants must be provided with oxygen only above 15,000 ft. The crew must also use it for the time beyond 30 minutes in the 12,500 to 14,000 ft band [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Waiting to feel hypoxia
The learner climbs past 12,500 ft planning oxygen 'when I need it'
Show the AC warning and set an altitude to start oxygen [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Oximeter as the trigger
The learner keeps the mask off until the reading drops
Teach the FAA caution against using it as the sole indicator [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Quoting the handbook, not the rule
'Between 12,500 and 14,000', 'everyone must have it'
Slow donning
The mask takes longer than 5 seconds to go on
Practice donning from time to time [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]]
Breathing fast after donning
Rapid breathing, tingling, dizziness on oxygen
100 percent, check the system, then slow the breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]
Leaky demand mask
Facial hair under the seal
Air seeps in past beards and mustaches; check the fit on the ground [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]] [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Pilot on a passenger mask
The pilot uses a passenger continuous-flow mask
Pilots use the masks meant for them [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Loose cylinder

Fasten it before flight [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]

Lip balm or greasy hands at the equipment
Wash hands; no petroleum products [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]
Valves left on
Regulator or bottle open after landing
Verify all components and valves are off [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]
Instructor error: a real decompression
Plan to dump cabin pressure to train
61.31(g) training simulates it without actually depressurizing [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]

body.p: This Task has no numeric tolerance. The examiner judges whether your briefing is adequate, whether you operate or simulate the equipment correctly, and whether your quantity answer fits the scenario (ACS AI.II.N.S1 to S3).

check.q: Your learner, on oxygen at 16,000 ft, reports tingling and dizziness and is breathing fast. What is the first fix you teach?
check.a: Set the regulator to 100 percent and check the system is working, then work on the rate and depth of breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

f1.caption: Table 2-5. Common hypoxia signs and symptoms. (AC 61-107B, page 20)
f1.alt: A two-column table. Signs: rapid breathing, cyanosis (bluing effect of the skin), poor coordination, lethargy, executing poor judgment, sweating, trembling, myoclonic (muscle) spasms. Symptoms: air hunger, fatigue, nausea, headache, dizziness, hot and cold flashes, tingling, visual impairment, euphoria.

f2.caption: Figure 2-3. Times of useful consciousness versus altitude. (AC 61-107B, page 24)
f2.alt: A curve shows TUC falling steeply as altitude increases, then flattening. Below it a table gives altitude, TUC, and TUC following rapid decompression: 18,000 ft 20 to 30 min, 10 to 15 min; 22,000 ft 10 min, 5 to 6 min; 25,000 ft 3 to 5 min, 1.5 to 2.5 min; 28,000 ft 2.5 to 3 min, 1 to 1.5 min; 30,000 ft 1 to 2 min, 30 s to 1 min; 35,000 ft 30 s to 1 min, 15 to 30 s; 40,000 ft 15 to 20 s, nominal; 43,000 and 50,000 ft 9 to 12 s, nominal.

f3.caption: Figure 7-43. Oxygen system regulator. (PHAK 7-37)
f3.alt: A black panel labeled Oxygen Regulator, Pressure Demand. It has a FLOW window, a red lever with Emergency, Normal and Test Mask positions, a white lever for 100% Oxygen or Normal Oxygen, a green Supply On and Off lever, and an oxygen supply pressure gauge in psi.

f4.alt: A three-column table. Traditional Teaching Process: Preparation, Presentation, Application, Review and Evaluation. Demonstration-Performance Method: Explanation, Demonstration, Learner performance supervision, Evaluation. Telling-and-Doing Technique: Preparation; Instructor tells, Instructor does; a highlighted Learner tells, Instructor does; Learner tells, Learner does; Learner does, Instructor evaluates.

f5.alt: A three-row table. Don mask: in 5 seconds or less, check for flow, breathe 100 percent oxygen. Descend: preferably below 10,000 ft. Land A.S.A.P.: at the nearest suitable installation where appropriate medical help can be found.

scenario.title: A new turboprop owner who 'always knows'
scenario.setup: Dana, a commercial pilot, has bought a pressurized single-engine turboprop whose AFM lists a maximum operating altitude of 30,000 ft and a service ceiling above that. She hires you to train her. She plans to fly her spouse and teenager at FL 270 with the cabin at about 10,000 ft. The airplane has a crew demand mask and continuous-flow passenger masks. She has never been in an altitude chamber and says she always knows when she is short of oxygen because she felt it hiking at 14,000 ft.

questions.q: What must Dana have before she acts as PIC of this airplane?
questions.a: Logged ground training in the nine 61.31(g)(1) subjects and flight training under 61.31(g)(2), each with an instructor endorsement, because the lower of service ceiling and maximum operating altitude is above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]. AC 61-65K A.74 gives sample wording [[12:54|AC 61-65K A.74]].

questions.q: How do you answer 'I always know when I'm short of oxygen'?
questions.a: AC 61-107B calls that idea a common, misleading and dangerous misconception [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Judgment degrades from the start [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]], and euphoria is probably the most dangerous symptom [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Recommend a chamber flight so she learns her own signature [[11:17|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

questions.q: At FL 270 with a 10,000 ft cabin, what does 91.211 require?
questions.a: No one has to use oxygen, because the cabin pressure altitude is below 12,500 ft. Because the airplane is above FL 250, a 10-minute supply must be available for each occupant, 3 x 10 = 30 occupant-minutes, on top of any paragraph (a) oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

questions.q: What limitation of the passengers' system do you brief?
questions.a: Continuous-flow systems are usually for passengers [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]] and need very careful attention above 25,000 ft MSL [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. After a decompression at FL 270 the cabin would be in that range, so the descent comes right after the masks.

questions.q: What TUC do you give her for a rapid decompression near FL 270?
questions.a: Figure 2-3 has no FL 270 row. Use the 28,000 ft row as the conservative bracket: 1 to 1.5 minutes after a rapid decompression, and plan on the lower value, 1 minute [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

questions.q: How do you teach her the mask drill?
questions.a: Telling-and-doing on the ground: you demonstrate, she tells while you do, then she does it while thinking aloud, then you evaluate [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. In flight, simulate the decompression without depressurizing [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]], and have her practice donning from time to time [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

skills.do: The examiner will ask you to "Provide an adequate briefing on use of supplemental oxygen equipment" (ACS AI.II.N.S1). There is no numeric tolerance. Brief as you would a learner or passenger: when oxygen goes on, how to don it and check flow, what to do if symptoms appear, no smoking or petroleum products, and the emergency drill.
skills.practice: Brief a non-pilot friend with the real equipment, then have them don it with no help. Check your briefing against the AC 61-107B emergency drill and fire precautions [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

skills.do: The examiner will ask you to "Operate or simulate operation of the installed or portable oxygen equipment in the aircraft, if installed or available" (ACS AI.II.N.S2). Expect to preflight, don, check flow, and shut off the system while explaining each step as you would to a learner.
skills.practice: Run the AFH functional test aloud: supply and pressure, regulator, flow, mask fit, microphone check [[24:309|AFH 15-15]]. Then teach it to a friend with telling-and-doing [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: The examiner will ask you to "Determine the quantity of supplemental oxygen required in a scenario given by the evaluator" (ACS AI.II.N.S3). There is no numeric tolerance. Show the profile by cabin pressure altitude, who must use and who must be provided with oxygen and for how long, any 10-minute pressurized reserve, and how you turn that into supply from the AFM chart.
skills.practice: Work three profiles on paper: a 13,500 ft cruise, a climb above 15,000 ft, and a pressurized flight above FL 250 [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Then convert each to supply with a real oxygen system duration chart.

quiz.q: About what share of the oxygen you inhale feeds the brain, per AC 61-107B?
quiz.why: Approximately 20 percent of all the oxygen you inhale feeds the brain [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of hypoxia in AC 61-107B Table 2-5, rather than a symptom?
quiz.why: Lethargy is in the signs column; the others are symptoms the person feels [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

quiz.q: Which hypoxia symptom does AC 61-107B call probably the least reliable?
quiz.why: Visual impairment is probably the least reliable, because the visual field changes so slowly it can go unnoticed [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

quiz.q: 61.31(g) applies to a pressurized aircraft when which number is above 25,000 ft MSL?
options: The lower of its service ceiling and maximum operating altitude
quiz.why: The rule says service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]].

quiz.q: How does 61.31(g)(2) say the rapid decompression is trained?
options: With a real depressurization above 25,000 ft
Simulated, without actually depressurizing the aircraft
It is not part of the training
quiz.why: Proper emergency procedures for simulated rapid decompression without actually depressurizing the aircraft [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]].

quiz.q: What is the minimum age to take the CAMI aviation physiology course?
quiz.why: Trainees must be at least 18 years of age [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

quiz.q: As a general rule, by how much does a rapid decompression to between 25,000 and 43,000 ft cut TUC?
quiz.why: TUC following decompression to altitudes between 25,000 and 43,000 ft is reduced by 50 percent [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

quiz.q: Which regulation requires altitude chamber training?
quiz.why: None of the regulations include altitude chamber training [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

quiz.q: In telling-and-doing, in which step is the learner passive?
quiz.why: The instructor's demonstration with explanation is the only step in which the learner plays a passive role [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

quiz.q: After an extreme hypoxia exposure, what can 100 percent oxygen do for 15 to 60 seconds?
quiz.why: It can cause an apparent increase in the severity of symptoms for 15 to 60 seconds; keep breathing 100 percent slowly [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner cruises 50 minutes with the cabin at exactly 14,000 ft, unpressurized, Part 91. How long must he use oxygen?
final_quiz.why: 14,000 ft is inside the band above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 ft, so the crew uses oxygen for the part beyond 30 minutes: 50 - 30 = 20 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

final_quiz.q: A learner plans 3 hours by day at exactly 12,500 ft cabin altitude, unpressurized. What is the best teaching answer?
options: Oxygen is required for the whole flight
91.211 does not require it, but the FAA recommends oxygen above 10,000 ft by day
final_quiz.why: The rule starts above 12,500 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. The FAA recommends supplemental oxygen to or above 10,000 ft by day [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says, 'I'll put the cannula on when my pulse oximeter starts dropping.' What does the FAA say?
options: Good plan; the oximeter is accurate to one percent
Do not rely on it as the sole indicator; waiting for it to fall can let impairment set in
Oximeters do not work at altitude
final_quiz.why: The FAA cautions against relying on pulse oximeters as the sole indicator of hypoxia: waiting can allow impairing hypoxia, and fingertip saturation may not reflect brain oxygen [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot did a part 135 PIC proficiency check in a pressurized aircraft and now wants to fly her own pressurized airplane with a 30,000 ft maximum operating altitude. Does she need your 61.31(g) endorsement?
options: No, if she can document that check
final_quiz.why: Completing a PIC proficiency check under part 121, 125 or 135 in a pressurized aircraft is one of the documented exceptions [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31]].

final_quiz.q: On oxygen in a pressurized airplane after a cabin fault, your learner breathes fast and reports tingling and dizziness. What first?
options: Set the regulator to 100 percent and check the system works
final_quiz.why: If a pilot on oxygen has symptoms, set the regulator to 100 percent and check the system before attending to breathing rate and depth [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

final_quiz.q: A learner had a chamber flight Monday at 0900 and wants to fly Monday at 1500. What does AC 61-107B say?
options: Wait at least 24 hours after chamber exposure
final_quiz.why: Allow at least 24 hours between hypobaric (altitude) chamber exposure and flying [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your passengers include two heavy smokers on a pressurized flight. What does AC 61-107B suggest?
options: Give them oxygen only above 15,000 ft
Let them smoke with masks off
final_quiz.why: If heavy smokers are aboard, a lower cabin altitude should be set, because their physiological altitudes are generally much higher than actual [[11:23|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:24|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: In a turbocharged pressurized piston single, oil temperature rises, oil pressure drops and manifold pressure falls at altitude. What extra risk do you teach?
options: Loss of cabin pressure if pressurization depends on the turbocharger, so watch for a slow decompression
final_quiz.why: These indicate a turbocharger problem; if pressurization depends on the turbocharger compressor, cabin pressure can be lost, so monitor it during the descent [[11:42|AC 61-107B 2-11a]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner lands after 4 hours unpressurized at 19,000 ft and plans a long, hard hike. What does AC 61-107B say?
options: Fine; DCS only happens in the air
Avoid strenuous activity for 24 hours after such a flight
Fine if she breathed 100 percent oxygen
final_quiz.why: Avoid unnecessary strenuous activity before flying unpressurized above 18,000 ft and for 24 hours after the flight [[11:34|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: On a Part 135 flight a passenger's medical oxygen bottle must be changed while passengers are aboard. Who may do it?
options: Only a person trained in the use of medical oxygen equipment
final_quiz.why: No one other than a person trained in the use of medical oxygen equipment may connect or disconnect bottles while any passenger is aboard [[6:27|14 CFR 135.91]].

final_quiz.q: You finish 61.31(g) training with a pilot. Which AC 61-65K sample endorsement fits?
final_quiz.why: A.74 is the endorsement to act as PIC in a pressurized aircraft capable of high-altitude operations; A.73 is high performance and A.75 tailwheel [[12:54|AC 61-65K A.74]].

final_quiz.q: In a simulator at 25,000 ft, your learner takes 12 seconds to don the mask after a simulated rapid decompression. Using the AC's lower TUC value, about what share of the budget did that use?
final_quiz.why: Lower value after rapid decompression at 25,000 ft is 1.5 min = 90 s [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]]; 12 / 90 = 0.133, about 13 percent, over twice the 5-second goal [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

final_quiz.q: At 14,500 ft without oxygen, your learner grows giggly and sure that everything is fine. What do you do?
options: Keep going; it is only 14,500 ft
Oxygen on, 100 percent; descend, preferably below 10,000 ft; land if symptoms persist
Wait for the oximeter to confirm
final_quiz.why: Euphoria is the most dangerous symptom [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Table 2-6: don mask, breathe 100 percent; descend preferably below 10,000 ft; land as soon as possible [[11:27|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

takeaways: Teach 91.211 from its words: cabin pressure altitude, required minimum flight crew, provided with and uses, each occupant provided with.

61.31(g) covers pressurized aircraft whose lower of service ceiling and maximum operating altitude is above 25,000 ft: nine ground subjects, flight training with a simulated decompression, and your endorsement.
Hypoxia takes judgment first and has no safe altitude line; believing you will notice it is the misconception to teach against.
Signs are for the observer and symptoms for the pilot; a chamber flight teaches a pilot's own signature, but no regulation requires one.
TUC is a budget, not the time to unconsciousness: use the lower number and halve it after a rapid decompression.
Sort systems by when oxygen flows, use only aviator's breathing oxygen (SAE AS8010), and secure the bottle away from oil and flame.
Teach the equipment with telling-and-doing on the ground, then simulate in flight with a clear exchange of controls.
cfi_notes: PHAK 7-37 paraphrases 91.211: flight crews 'have and use' oxygen 'between 12,500 and 14,000 feet' and every occupant above 15,000 ft 'must have' it [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. The rule says required minimum flight crew, above 12,500 ft up to and including 14,000 ft, and each occupant 'provided with' [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. Teach the CFR wording.

61.31(g)(1) describes an endorsement for the ground training and 61.31(g)(2) one for flight proficiency [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]], while AC 61-65K gives one combined sample, A.74 [[12:54|AC 61-65K A.74]]. If you give the ground training separately, record it then; the sources give no separate ground-only sample.

PHAK Figure 17-1 lists 5 to 10 minutes at 22,000 ft and '30 minutes or more' at 20,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. AC 61-107B gives 10 minutes at 22,000 ft and says to use the lower value [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]], and the AIM says corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Teach the AIM and AC 61-107B numbers.

The PHAK says a rapid decompression cuts effective performance time 'by one-third to one-fourth its normal time' [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. AC 61-107B says by 50 percent between 25,000 and 43,000 ft, and 'at least 50 percent' elsewhere [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]] [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Teach 'at least half'.

The PHAK lists cyanosis among hypoxia symptoms [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; AC 61-107B puts it under signs, which an observer detects [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]]. Use the AC split; it tells an instructor what to watch for.
The ACS says 'demand' systems; the PHAK and AC 61-107B call them diluter-demand [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. Teach both names so learners recognize either.
The AIM and AC 61-107B give different CAMI phone numbers and older web addresses [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[11:36|AC 61-107B 2-8]]. Check current contact details on faa.gov before you send a learner.
A learner who dons a mask in flight is heads-down. Brief the positive exchange of flight controls before every donning drill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

The AFH turboprop outline lists 'effects of prolonged oxygen use' and 61.31(g)(1)(v) requires it as a ground subject [[24:308|AFH 15-14]] [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]], but none of the PHAK, AIM, AFH or AC 61-107B explains the effects. Use an AME or aviation medicine text and say so.
gaps: Effects of prolonged use of supplemental oxygen: a required 61.31(g)(1) subject, not explained in the PHAK, AIM, AFH or AC 61-107B.

How to physically identify aviator's breathing oxygen against medical or industrial oxygen (cylinder markings, supplier certificates, moisture content) is not described beyond the SAE AS8010 standard.

Flow rates and duration charts: apart from one AC 61-107B example (22 cubic ft, about 1.5 hours, four people at 18,000 ft) [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]], supply planning needs the AFM supplement or the system maker's chart.
Hydrostatic test intervals and cylinder markings are not given; AC 61-107B says only that a DOT-approved facility must test the bottles before use [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].
No target oxygen saturation number for a pulse oximeter, and no guidance on portable or simulator-based hypoxia trainers; ask an AME.
Regulator positions, donning steps and emergency descent speeds for a given airplane come from its AFM/POH [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

activities.title: Which source says it?
activities.intro: Tap a source, then what it says.

pairs.r: Simulated rapid decompression without actually depressurizing
None of the regulations include altitude chamber training
Symptoms of hypoxia do not vary in an individual
Sample endorsement for PIC of a pressurized aircraft capable of high-altitude operations
Each occupant provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft cabin altitude
Functional test includes ATC communication using mask microphones

activities.title: Rule or recommendation?
activities.intro: Tap each item, then whether 14 CFR requires it or the FAA only recommends it.

items.t: Required crew use oxygen beyond 30 minutes above 12,500 up to 14,000 ft
Each occupant provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft
A 10-minute supply per occupant above FL 250, pressurized
Ground training in respiration and hypoxia before PIC of a qualifying pressurized aircraft
Descend below 10,000 ft if hypoxia is suspected

activities.title: True or false: what learners believe about hypoxia
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Most pilots can recognize hypoxia and correct it before they are seriously impaired.
cards.why: False. AC 61-107B calls this a common misconception that is misleading and dangerous [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

cards.s: The order and intensity of your own hypoxia symptoms usually stay the same over the years.
cards.why: True. That is the greatest benefit of chamber training [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

cards.s: An observer can often detect signs of hypoxia that the hypoxic pilot cannot use to recognize it.
cards.why: True. Signs can be detected by an observer and are not effective for self-recognition [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

cards.s: A healthy pilot is never affected by hypoxia below 12,000 ft MSL.
cards.why: False. There is no assurance, and impairment is a continuum with no definite starting altitude [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

cards.s: Time of useful consciousness is the time until the pilot passes out.
cards.why: False. TUC is not the onset of unconsciousness; impaired performance may be immediate [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

cards.s: Hyperventilation can be an early response to hypoxia at altitude.
cards.why: True. Hyperventilation occurs as an early adaptive mechanism to hypoxia, which makes the two hard to tell apart [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

activities.title: What each control on the regulator does
activities.intro: Drag each job to the part of the regulator that does it.

pins.label: Shows whether oxygen is moving to the mask
Shows how much oxygen is left in the supply
Selects 100 percent oxygen for high altitude
Turns the oxygen supply on or off
Emergency, normal or test mask positions

activities.why: Panel from PHAK Figure 7-43 [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Crewmembers should select 100 percent at high altitude [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]; check flow, quantity and gauges on every preflight [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

activities.title: Training a turboprop owner, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are giving 61.31(g) training to a commercial pilot who bought a pressurized single-engine turboprop with a 30,000 ft maximum operating altitude. Make each call as her instructor.

steps.s: Planning the ground training. What must it include?
options: At least the nine 61.31(g)(1) subjects, such as respiration, hypoxia, duration of consciousness and decompression
steps.why: 61.31(g)(1) lists the subjects [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]. No regulation includes chamber training, though it is recommended [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

steps.s: She took a CAMI chamber flight yesterday at 1600. It is now 1000 and she wants to start the flight lesson.
options: Go if her oximeter reads normal
steps.why: Allow at least 24 hours between chamber exposure and flying [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

steps.s: Preflight. What goes into the oxygen functional test?
options: Supply and pressure, regulator, flow, mask fit, and talking to ATC through the mask microphone
Nothing; it is checked in flight
steps.why: The AFH outline lists all of these [[24:309|AFH 15-15]]; AC 61-107B also has you demonstrate crew and ATC communication with the oxygen equipment [[11:44|AC 61-107B 2-12]].

steps.s: At FL 260 you want to train a rapid decompression.
options: Dump the cabin pressure to make it real
Announce a simulated decompression; she dons her mask at once and flies the emergency descent
Have her remove her mask to feel symptoms
steps.why: 61.31(g)(2) requires simulated rapid decompression without actually depressurizing, and emergency descent procedures [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]. The AFH pairs it with immediate donning [[24:309|AFH 15-15]].

steps.s: After landing, she is proficient. What do you do?
options: Endorse her logbook or training record, for example with AC 61-65K A.74
steps.why: 61.31(g) requires endorsements in the logbook or training record [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31]]; A.74 is the sample [[12:54|AC 61-65K A.74]].

activities.title: The 61.31(g) training flight, in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put AC 61-107B's flight training outline in order, then tap Check.
steps: Preflight inspection, including setup and functional test of the oxygen system
Climb and normal cruise above 25,000 ft MSL
Simulated emergencies: rapid decompression and emergency descent

activities.title: Work the oxygen numbers you will teach
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Part 91, unpressurized: 70 minutes with the cabin at 13,500 ft. For how many minutes must the required crew use oxygen?
items.why: Only the part beyond 30 minutes in the band above 12,500 up to 14,000 ft: 70 - 30 = 40 [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

items.q: A pressurized airplane at FL 270 carries 5 occupants. How many occupant-minutes of descent oxygen must be available beyond paragraph (a)?
items.why: At least a 10-minute supply for each occupant above FL 250: 5 x 10 = 50 [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

items.q: AC 61-107B: a 22 cubic ft container lasts about 1.5 hours for four people at 18,000 ft. About how many cubic ft per person-hour is that?
At that same rate, about how many hours would the same container last for two people at 18,000 ft? (Application: assumes use per person stays the same.)
At 25,000 ft TUC is 3 to 5 minutes. Halve the lower value for a rapid decompression. How many seconds is that?
items.why: 3 min x 0.5 = 1.5 min = 90 s, matching the 1.5 to 2.5 min rapid-decompression column [[11:29|AC 61-107B 2-7]].

items.q: A trip would use 12 cubic ft on continuous flow. Pulse demand saves 50 to 85 percent. At the smallest saving, what is the most it would use?
